content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) encompasses a group of inherited hemoglobin disorders that can affect multiple organs, including the eyes. Some individuals with SCD develop ocular complications, with vision-threatening issues primarily arising from proliferative sickle retinopathy (PSR). PSR is characterized by the abnormal growth of new blood vessels in the retina. Laser photocoagulation is a widely used treatment for proliferative retinopathies, and its efficacy and safety in managing PSR need to be evaluated to prevent sight-threatening complications. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of various laser photocoagulation techniques in treating SCD-related proliferative retinopathy. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group’s Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, LILACS, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platforms, and ClinicalTrials.gov. The last search was conducted in June and July 2022. Randomized controlled trials comparing laser photocoagulation to no treatment in children and adults with SCD were included. Three trials involving 414 eyes from 339 participants (160 males and 179 females, aged 13 to 67 years) were included in the review. These trials compared the efficacy and safety of laser photocoagulation to no treatment in PSR. Different laser techniques were used: one trial employed sectoral scatter laser photocoagulation with an argon laser, another used feeder vessel coagulation with argon laser in one center and xenon arc in another, and the third trial used focal scatter laser photocoagulation with an argon laser. The follow-up periods ranged from 21 to 48 months across the trials. Two trials had a high risk of allocation bias due to the randomization method for participants with bilateral disease, while the third trial had an unclear risk of selection bias. One trial was also at risk of reporting bias. Since the unit of analysis was the eye rather than the individual, the data were reported narratively. In the trial using sectoral scatter laser photocoagulation (174 eyes), there was no significant difference between the laser and control groups in terms of complete regression of PSR (30.2% in the laser group vs. 22.4% in the control group) or the development of new PSR (34.3% in the laser group vs. 41.3% in the control group). The certainty of this evidence was graded as very low. In the two-center trial using feeder vessel coagulation, data from one center (mean follow-up of nine years) showed no significant difference in the development of new sea fan neovascularization between the treated group (48.0%) and the control group (45.0%, P = 0.64). Another trial reported regression of PSR in 55% of the laser group compared to 28.6% of controls, and progression of PSR in 10.5% of treated eyes versus 25.7% of control eyes. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was also graded as very low. Regarding visual loss, the sectoral scatter laser trial reported a lower incidence in treated eyes (3.0%) compared to control eyes (12.0%) over a mean follow-up of 47 and 42 months, respectively (P = 0.019). The feeder vessel coagulation trial reported visual loss in 1.14% of treated eyes versus 7.5% of control eyes (mean follow-up of 26 to 32 months, P = 0.07). The focal scatter laser trial reported stable visual acuity in 72/73 treated eyes, with visual loss occurring in only one control eye. The certainty of evidence for visual outcomes was graded as very low. Vitreous hemorrhage was reported in 12.0% of treated eyes versus 25.3% of control eyes in the sectoral scatter laser trial (mean follow-up of 42 to 47 months, P ≤ 0.05). In the feeder vessel coagulation trial, vitreous hemorrhage occurred in 3.4% of treated eyes versus 27.5% of control eyes (mean follow-up of 26 to 32 months). At one center with a nine-year follow-up, vitreous hemorrhage was observed in 4.0% of treated eyes compared to 45.0% of control eyes (P = 0.002). The focal scatter laser trial reported no vitreous hemorrhage in the treated group, while 17.1% of control eyes experienced this complication. The certainty of evidence for vitreous hemorrhage was graded as low. Adverse effects were minimal. One case of retinal tear was reported. Retinal detachment was observed in all three trials, but there was no significant difference between the treatment and control groups. One trial reported an increased risk of choroidal neovascularization with xenon arc treatment, but visual loss from this complication was rare with long-term follow-up of three years or more. Other adverse effects and quality-of-life outcomes were not reported. The authors concluded that the available evidence, much of which is over 30 years old and of low or very low certainty, does not provide sufficient clarity on whether laser therapy for PSR improves clinical outcomes. Laser treatment does not appear to significantly affect outcomes such as regression of PSR or the development of new lesions. No evidence was available regarding patient-important outcomes, such as quality of life or the ability to maintain a driving license. Further research is needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of laser therapy compared to other interventions, such as intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs). Future studies should also address patient-important outcomes and cost-effectiveness.
